newsitem.title: republic of ireland: Irish govt proposes Robinson for U.N. rights job.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt proposes Robinson for U.N. rights job.

text.p: The Irish government said on Wednesday that it was formally nominating its first woman President, Mary Robinson, for the job of U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights and would "actively support her candidature in every possible way."
The government's formal endorsement, which was expected, cleared the way for Robinson to seek one of the U.N.'s top jobs when her term of office expires later this year.

Robinson said last week that she would not be standing for re-election after almost eight years, prompting a wave of speculation that she would seek a United Nations position that suited her interests in human rights and the developing world.
Irish government support for her candidature was announced as Robinson visited the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia in The Hague, the first head of state to do so.
It also follows weekend expressions of support for her to seek the job from the White House, which has taken a tough stand towards reform and cost-saving at the United Nations.
Robinson said in a weekend interview that she would be interested in the U.N. human rights job if it became vacant and said Prime Minister John Bruton had promised support.
Even domestic critics say she combines a compassionate heart with legal skill and has left her stamp on the Irish presidency in a way that few before her have done.
A trained constitutional lawyer, Robinson became, in Bruton's words, the most popular Irish President of all time with a personal style that captured even the most begrudging hearts and minds.
She championed the causes of the less well-off and the disadvantaged, but most of all was an ambassadress for Ireland and its world-wide diaspora of more than 40 million.
Robinson was the first head of state to visit Somalia in 1992 and went to the United Nations to puts its drought, famine and civil war at the top of the international agenda.
Last month she re-visited Rwanda to show support for efforts to rebuild the country after genocide.
